newsitem.title: UK: Lira under the mark's gun in late Europe.
newsitem.headline: Lira under the mark's gun in late Europe.

text.p: The lira crumbled against the mark in late Europe as EMU jitters kicked in again ahead of Wednesday's release of EU 1997/98 economic forecasts.
U.S. institutions bought mark/lira in size, unsettled by suggestions the idea of a "core" EMU -- excluding Italy -- was gaining currency, traders said.
"It looks like the U.S. and European institutions are basically disinvesting from Italy for the time being," said a chief EMS trader at a Japanese bank here.
Bundesbank vice-president Johann-Wilhelm Gaddum said earlier it would be no problem launching EMU with a smaller group.
"There's nothing wrong with starting with a smaller range of participants if that makes it easier to launch a real community of stability," Gaddum told a Tokyo symposium on EMU.
Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer spoke in similar vein on Monday, saying EMU stood the best chance of succeeding if it was led by a "homogeneous" group of states.
"The talk...about a core EMU lends disenchantment with existing convergence trades on Italian assets and will lead to capital flows from Italy in the short term," the trader said.
The lira hit a low of 998.85 per mark in Europe, recovering to 997.45/75 by 1415 GMT but down from late Monday's 995.00/50.
The European Commission's 1997/98 forecasts, which cover inflation, budget deficits, debt levels and GDP, are due to appear on Wednesday.
The Commission is expected to forecast that only Italy and Greece could miss the 3.0 percent deficit/GDP ratio targeted in the Maastricht Treaty on monetary union.

The lira's weakness was likely to preclude the Bank of Italy interest rate cut which Italy so badly needs, analysts said. Data from six Italian cities yesterday indicated a preliminary year-on-year CPI rate of 1.8 percent -- a healthy level which opened the door to monetary easing, analysts said.

The French franc found some composure as campaigning for the May 25/June 1 election kicked off. But analysts warned that market fears of a Socialist win -- and a possibly reduced commitment to EMU -- would cap the French currency for now.
French President Jacques Chirac called the snap election late on Monday, in a bid to give the government a clear run up to the proposed launch of the euro on January 1, 1999.

"The French election looks like it's turning into a second referendum. It will be test of France's fiscal resolve and there is some risk to the EMU project," said Thomas Rayner, international economist at SGST in London.
The franc was trading at 3.3745/47 per mark at 1441 GMT versus 3.3769/71 in late Europe yesterday.
Bundesbank head Tietmeyer offered the mark some support earlier in the session, saying a delayed EMU launch could be considered if big countries missed the entry criteria.
But traders said the market impact was softened by Tietmeyer's remark that the Bundesbank was operating on the assumption that currency union would begin on schedule.
Elsewhere, Germany's six top economic research institutes released their widely-leaked spring report, predicting Germany's 1997 budget deficit at 3.0 to 3.2 percent.

The institutes foresaw Bundesbank interest rates staying steady this year, with a small tightening in early 1998. Buba council member Franz-Christoph Zeitler said there was no reason for an upturn in German rates in the foreseeable future.
Zeitler also said there was no longer a need for major currencies to correct against the mark.
-- Abigail Levene, London Newsroom +44-171-542-8968
